report:
### Conclusion
Extensive scientific evidence demonstrates that increasing the number of childhood vaccines or receiving multiple vaccine antigens does not cause or increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

### Summary of Evidence

1. **Cumulative Vaccine Burden:** Research evaluating early childhood exposure to vaccine antigens found no association between the cumulative number of vaccine antigens received and the subsequent development of autism (https://www.healthday.com/health-news/conditions/another-study-sees-no-vaccine-autism-link-674876.html).
2. **Systematic Meta-Analyses:** A comprehensive meta-analysis by Taylor et al. synthesized data from cohort and case-control studies involving over one million children. It concluded that vaccinations, specific components (such as thimerosal), and combination vaccines are not associated with the development of autism or ASD (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/).
3. **Schedule Safety Reviews:** An extensive evaluation by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) examined scientific evidence regarding the safety of the federal childhood immunization schedule and affirmed its safety, finding no evidence linking the schedule to autism (https://www.academicpedsjnl.net/article/S1876-2859(13)00159-9/fulltext).
4. **Public Health Consensus:** Major medical and public health organizations consistently emphasize that rigorous epidemiological studies show no scientific link between administering recommended childhood vaccines and developing autism (https://www.immunize.org/clinical/vaccine-confidence/topic/mmr-vaccine/).

The belief that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism is contradicted by robust scientific consensus.
